questions.decision: The 'feel safe' ambiguity in the brief was never opened â€” none of the three loss-mode options (server restore, local draft, warn-before-unload) shows up in the touched files, so the candidate implicitly scoped data-safety out or believes it was already covered.
questions.question: The brief asked for the editor to 'feel safe.' Walk me through what data-loss scenario you decided that meant â€” a reload mid-edit, a failed save, a closed tab â€” and which one you deliberately chose not to handle. What would a user have to lose before you'd change that scoping?
questions.listenFor: Names concrete loss modes unprompted, admits which one they punted on and why (time-box, existing flush cadence felt sufficient), can describe the trade-off between server-restore and local-draft reconciliation in terms of stale-overwrite risk.
questions.redFlag: Claims safety was 'handled' without naming a mechanism, or discovers live that they never considered reload-mid-edit; describes all three options as equally fine with no reason for the one shipped.

questions.decision: The existing flush()/re-buffer pipeline and the append-only hash-chained event log were left untouched â€” either a deliberate 'don't break the integrity contract' call or the code was never read.
questions.question: The session capture path has an append-only event log with an integrity chain behind it. Open that flush logic with me now â€” before you look: what did you understand its contract to be when you worked around it, and what change did you consider making there that you decided was too risky?
questions.listenFor: Can orient in the file quickly, articulates the ordering/append-only invariant in their own words, names a concrete rejected change (e.g. adding a restore read path) and the re-verification cost that made them avoid it.
questions.redFlag: Visibly reading the file for the first time; describes the pipeline only in the generic terms an assistant summary would use; cannot say what would break if events were re-appended out of order.

questions.decision: Verification signal exists in the trace (2 explicit verify asks to the assistant) but the known failure paths â€” retry double-appending a re-buffered batch, restore clobbering newer local edits â€” were not exercised in the probe area.
questions.question: You asked your tools to check their own output a couple of times. Pick one of those checks: what specifically were you suspicious of, what did the check come back with, and was it right? Then tell me one failure path in this submission you know is NOT covered â€” what would it take to reproduce it by hand?
questions.listenFor: Recalls the actual suspicion that triggered the verify ask, can judge whether the model's self-check was trustworthy, and names an honest uncovered path (retry/replay, conflicting local vs server state) with a concrete repro recipe.
questions.redFlag: Cannot remember what was being verified or why; equates 'the model said it's fine' with verified; claims everything is covered, or names an uncovered path only in vague terms ('edge cases').

questions.decision: The prompt trace shows 8 iterative assistant prompts (~254 chars each, iteration depth 8, zero brief-pasting) but 0 clarifying questions and only 1 stakeholder question â€” the task was decomposed solo rather than de-ambiguated.
questions.question: Your working style here was many short, iterative prompts rather than pasting the brief in. Reconstruct that decomposition for me: what was your first prompt about, and at which step did the plan change from what you originally intended? Why didn't any ambiguity in the brief rise to the level of asking the stakeholder?
questions.listenFor: Can replay the actual sequence and point to a real pivot mid-way; gives a defensible reason for not asking (the ambiguity had a reversible default, they time-boxed a bet) rather than not noticing the ambiguity existed.
questions.redFlag: Cannot reconstruct their own prompt sequence or describes it generically ('I just asked it to build the feature'); the absence of clarifying questions turns out to be unawareness of the ambiguity rather than a judged bet.
